trust: Standards read, not summarised from ads

cta.p: Everything decoded here is stocked as certified garments and PPE, embroidered where it makes sense.

pages.cardBlurb: Type A, B and C, the letter codes, breakthrough times — and why the glove material matters more than the rating.
pages.h1: EN ISO 374: chemical gloves, letter by letter.
pages.metaTitle: EN ISO 374 Chemical Gloves Explained: Types & Letter Codes | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN ISO 374 decoded — Type A/B/C chemical gloves, what the letter codes under the beaker pictogram mean, breakthrough times, the virus marking, and how to match glove polymer to the actual chemical.
pages.lede: Chemical gloves carry the most information-dense marking in PPE: a pictogram, a type letter and a string of code letters that name the chemicals the glove actually resisted in testing. Read properly, the label answers the only question that matters — will this glove survive this substance long enough?

heroMeta.l: Each letter is a named chemical
Protection is a time, not a yes

blocks.html:
EN ISO 374-1 grades chemical gloves by how many of its standard test chemicals they resist, and for how long. Type A: at least 6 chemicals for 30+ minutes each. Type B: at least 3 chemicals, 30+ minutes. Type C: at least 1 chemical, 10+ minutes — splash-brief protection only. The letters printed under the beaker pictogram identify which chemicals passed: each code letter (A–T) is a named substance — A is methanol, K is sodium hydroxide (caustic), J is n-heptane, and so on through the list.

Breakthrough time is the honest number: it's how long the chemical takes to permeate the glove at molecular level — invisible, and unrelated to visible damage. A glove rated 30 minutes against caustic is a 30-minute glove, however intact it looks. Degradation (the material swelling or hardening) is tested separately, and disposable nitrile against a named solvent may be a minutes glove: right for a splash-and-doff task, wrong for immersion.

faq.q: What do the letters on chemical gloves mean?
faq.a: Each letter under the beaker pictogram is a specific test chemical from the EN ISO 374-1 list — A is methanol, K is sodium hydroxide, J is n-heptane and so on. The letters shown are the chemicals that glove resisted for the required breakthrough time in testing; match them against the substances you actually handle.

faq.q: What is the difference between Type A, B and C chemical gloves?
faq.a: Test breadth and duration: Type A resisted at least six of the standard chemicals for 30+ minutes each, Type B at least three for 30+ minutes, and Type C at least one for 10+ minutes. Type C is short-splash protection; sustained chemical work wants Type A in the right polymer.

faq.q: How long do chemical gloves protect for?
faq.a: Until breakthrough — the tested time the chemical takes to permeate the material, which happens invisibly and regardless of visible condition. Track the time in contact, not the look of the glove, and treat the manufacturer's per-chemical permeation data as the real specification.

pages.cardTitle: EN ISO 13688: the standard behind every standard
pages.cardBlurb: The general-requirements standard cited on every protective garment — sizing, innocuousness, marking and what it guarantees.
pages.h1: EN ISO 13688: the small print on every label.
pages.metaTitle: EN ISO 13688 Explained: Protective Clothing General Requirements | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN ISO 13688 decoded — the general-requirements standard cited alongside every protective clothing spec: innocuousness, ergonomics, sizing designation, marking rules and ageing information.
pages.lede: Look at any certified garment's label and one number appears alongside the headline standard, every time: EN ISO 13688. It's the general-requirements standard — never certified alone, always cited with — and it quietly guarantees the things you'd otherwise never think to check.

heroMeta.l: It has no protection claims itself
Safe materials, honest sizing, clear marking

blocks.h2: What the partner standard actually covers
blocks.html:
Protection standards like EN ISO 20471 or EN ISO 11612 define performance against a hazard. EN ISO 13688 defines everything else a protective garment must get right: innocuousness (materials can't themselves harm the wearer — pH limits, banned azo dyes, no known-harmful substances against skin), ergonomics (the garment must allow the work), sizing (declared against actual body dimensions, not vanity labels), marking (durable, legible, with the right pictograms), and manufacturer information (care, ageing and storage guidance must be supplied).

It matters to buyers in one practical way: a garment citing a protection standard without EN ISO 13688 alongside is mis-labelled or worse — the pairing is how the system is designed, and its absence is a counterfeit tell.

faq.q: What is EN ISO 13688?
faq.a: The general-requirements standard for protective clothing — covering innocuousness of materials, ergonomics, sizing designation, marking and manufacturer information. It's always certified in combination with a specific protection standard (hi-vis, FR, chemical), never alone, and it's the reason those basics are trustworthy on certified kit.

faq.q: Why does my hi-vis label say EN ISO 13688 as well as EN ISO 20471?
faq.a: Because the system pairs them deliberately: EN ISO 20471 covers the visibility performance, EN ISO 13688 covers the garment fundamentals — safe materials, honest sizing, durable marking, supplied care information. Every certified protective garment carries its protection standard plus 13688.

faq.q: Does EN ISO 13688 mean a garment is protective?
faq.a: No — by itself it makes no protection claim at all. A garment marked only with EN ISO 13688 is certified as safe, well-made clothing, not as PPE against any hazard. The protection comes from the partner standard cited alongside it.

pages.cardBlurb: The -B suffix on protective coveralls decoded — barrier tests, type ratings and where biological protection actually applies.
pages.h1: EN 14126: the B on the label.
pages.metaTitle: EN 14126 Explained: Protective Clothing Against Infective Agents | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN 14126 decoded — what the -B suffix on coverall type ratings means, the four biological barrier tests, and where infective-agent protection applies: healthcare, waste, emergency response and labs.
pages.lede: After 2020, everyone has seen the suits; almost nobody can read their labels. EN 14126 is the standard that turns a chemical coverall into biological PPE — the difference between Type 5/6 and Type 5-B/6-B is one letter and four barrier tests, and knowing where it genuinely applies stops both under- and over-buying.

heroMeta.l: Biological barrier, added to a chem type
Blood, contact, wet and dry routes
Route of exposure picks the type

blocks.h2: A suffix that rides on the chemical types
blocks.html:
EN 14126 doesn't define its own garment shapes — it adds biological barrier performance to the existing chemical-suit types. A Type 6 splash coverall that also passes the biological tests becomes Type 6-B; a Type 5 particulate suit becomes 5-B; and so on up the scale. The tests behind the B cover the routes infection actually travels: resistance to penetration by contaminated liquids under pressure (synthetic blood), by mechanical contact with contaminated surfaces, by contaminated liquid aerosols, and by contaminated solid particles (dry dust).

Class levels within each test grade the performance — higher class, tougher barrier — and the garment's documentation states them. The practical read: match the type to the route. Splashing fluids point at 4-B/6-B liquid barriers; dry contaminated dust points at 5-B; heavy fluid exposure climbs to 3-B.

faq.q: What does Type 5-B or 6-B mean on a coverall?
faq.a: The number is the chemical-suit type (5 = particulates, 6 = light splash); the B means the fabric also passed EN 14126's biological barrier tests against contaminated liquids, aerosols, dust and contact. Same garment shapes, added infective-agent performance.

faq.q: Is EN 14126 the same as medical PPE?
faq.a: It overlaps but isn't identical — EN 14126 covers protective clothing against infective agents generally (industrial, emergency and clinical settings), while medical devices like surgical gowns follow their own standards. In workplace infection-risk settings, the -B coverall types are the usual specification.

faq.q: Do I need EN 14126 for handling sewage?
faq.a: Wastewater and flood-response work commonly specifies liquid-barrier types with the B suffix (4-B or 6-B depending on exposure), alongside gauntlets, wellingtons and strict hygiene routines. The employer's risk assessment sets the exact type; the B is what makes the barrier claim biological, not just chemical.

pages.cardBlurb: Antistatic, ESD and conductive are three different specs — the resistance ranges, the standards and who needs which.
pages.h1: ESD footwear: three specs that get called one name.
pages.metaTitle: ESD Footwear & EN 61340 Explained: Antistatic vs ESD vs Conductive | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: ESD footwear decoded — the difference between antistatic (A-rated), ESD (EN 61340) and conductive footwear, the resistance ranges behind each, and which spec electronics, battery and ATEX work actually needs.
pages.lede: Three different footwear specs get sold under one careless word: the antistatic A in a safety-boot code, the ESD symbol from the electronics world, and conductive footwear for explosive atmospheres. They're defined by different resistance ranges, serve different masters — and swapping one for another quietly breaks the system it was part of.

blocks.html:
All three specs manage the same thing — charge flowing from body to ground through the sole — but each defines its own resistance window. Antistatic (the A in codes like S1P, tested under the safety footwear standards) is the broad general-industry band: enough dissipation to prevent nuisance sparks, plenty of resistance left for electrical-shock reasons. ESD footwear (tested to the EN 61340 family, worn in electronics and battery production) sits in a tighter, lower window: charge bleeds away fast enough to protect components that die at voltages a human can't even feel — it's product protection, verified with tester stations at the door. Conductive footwear is the lowest-resistance case, for specialist explosive-atmosphere work where any retained charge is intolerable — and it's specified by the site, never casually, precisely because it removes the shock-protection resistance the other types keep.

The garment side pairs with it: EN 1149-5 clothing in ATEX zones, ESD smocks in electronics — and none of it works over an insulating floor. It's a system: footwear, flooring, garment, sometimes wrist strap, engineered together.

head: Spec
Protects
Where it lives
rows: Against nuisance static; keeps shock resistance
General industry default — most S1P/S3 boots have it
The clothing half of the same system

items.l: An antistatic site boot usually won't pass an electronics plant's tester station — buy to the zone's spec

faq.q: What is the difference between antistatic and ESD footwear?
faq.a: Resistance range and purpose. Antistatic (the A in safety-boot codes) is a broad band that prevents nuisance static while keeping shock-protective resistance — the general-industry default. ESD footwear meets the tighter, lower EN 61340 window that protects sensitive electronics, verified at tester stations. An ordinary antistatic boot frequently fails an ESD test.

faq.q: Who needs ESD safety shoes?
faq.a: Staff in ESD-protected areas: electronics assembly, semiconductor and battery production, and some lab and cleanroom environments — anywhere static discharge damages the product rather than the person. The site's ESD programme specifies the footwear and usually tests it daily.

faq.q: Why did my ESD shoes fail the tester?
faq.a: The path broke somewhere: worn or contaminated soles, insulating aftermarket insoles, very dry skin, or thick synthetic socks. Most failures fix with cleaning the soles, the correct insoles, or ESD-compatible socks — and testers exist precisely to catch this before you touch a board.

pages.cardBlurb: EN ISO 20345:2022 changed the codes — S1PL and S1PS arrived, slip ratings were rewritten, and both labels are in shops now.
pages.metaTitle: EN ISO 20345:2022 Explained: New Safety Boot Codes & Slip Ratings | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: The 2022 safety footwear update decoded — S1PL and S1PS midsole codes, the rewritten slip-resistance system (SR baseline, SC scuff cap, LG ladder grip), and why old and new labels share shelves.
pages.lede: Safety footwear's rulebook was revised in 2022, and the shelves now carry two generations of labels: boots certified to the 2011 edition still sold legitimately alongside 2022-certified kit whose codes look subtly different. Nothing was recalled and nothing old became unsafe — but a buyer reading S1PS for the first time deserves the translation.

blocks.html:
The headline: perforation-resistant midsoles got honest letters. Under the old system, S1P said 'midsole' without saying which kind. The 2022 edition splits it: S1PS means a steel midsole, S1PL a textile one tested against a larger, more realistic nail — ending the quiet ambiguity our boot-codes guide and composite-vs-steel pages have always had to explain. S6 and S7 join the ladder as waterproof versions of S2 and S3 logic.

Slip resistance was rebuilt. The old SRA/SRB/SRC trio is retired: baseline slip performance is now mandatory for certification (tested on ceramic with detergent), with an optional SR marking for the tougher glycerine test — plus new optional codes like SC (scuff-cap abrasion) and LG (ladder grip) for trades that need them.

What didn't change: toe protection is still 200 joules, the familiar S1–S5 ladder still reads the same way, and 2011-certified boots remain legal to sell and wear while certificates run — which is why both label styles will share shelves for years yet.

faq.q: What does S1PS and S1PL mean on safety boots?
faq.a: They're the 2022 split of the old S1P: S1PS has a steel perforation-resistant midsole, S1PL a non-metal textile one tested against a smaller-diameter nail than before. Protection intent is the same; the letters finally say which construction you're getting.

faq.q: Are SRA and SRC slip ratings still valid?
faq.a: On boots certified to the 2011 edition, yes, while those certificates run. The 2022 edition retired the SRA/SRB/SRC system: baseline slip resistance became mandatory for certification, with an optional tougher SR marking. You'll see both systems on shelves during the transition.

faq.q: Do I need to replace boots certified to the old standard?
faq.a: No — the 2022 revision changed testing and labelling for new certifications; it didn't invalidate existing kit. Replace boots on condition and fit as always. For new fleet specifications, writing requirements in the 2022 codes avoids ambiguity.

pages.cardBlurb: EN 361 harnesses to EN 360 blocks — what each number covers, the inspection duty, and how clothing fits around it all.
pages.h1: Fall protection standards: the map, honestly told.
pages.metaTitle: Fall Protection Standards Explained: EN 361, 355, 360 & More | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: The fall-protection standard family mapped — EN 361 harnesses, EN 355 energy absorbers, EN 360 retractables, EN 358 restraint — plus the inspection duties and how workwear interacts with a harness.
pages.lede: Fall-arrest equipment is the one PPE family we'd tell you not to buy casually: it's employer-provided, formally inspected, training-dependent kit whose standards are worth understanding even though the procurement belongs to competent hands. Here's the honest map — including where ordinary workwear fits into it.

heroMeta.l: What an absorber limits force to
Formal checks are part of the kit

blocks.html:
EN 361 is the full-body harness — the only body-holding device permitted for fall arrest. EN 355 covers energy-absorbing lanyards: the tearing element that limits arrest force to survivable levels. EN 360 is retractable fall arresters (the 'blocks'). EN 358 covers work-positioning and restraint — belts and lanyards that stop you reaching the edge at all, which is always the preferred design. EN 362 is connectors, EN 353 guided arresters on rails and lines, EN 341 descent and rescue devices. Every item is Category III PPE: certified with ongoing production oversight, used only with training, and subject to pre-use checks plus formal periodic inspection — at least annually, recorded, by a competent person (our inspection guide covers the paperwork side).

Where workwear fits: clothing is the interface between body and harness. Slim, fitted layers keep the harness geometry right; bulky padding under leg straps changes fit dangerously; loose hoods foul dorsal points; and trouser kit must not cover or catch the leg buckles. That's the practical guidance in our scaffolder and height-trade pages — and it's why we talk about fall protection at all despite not being the people to sell it to you.

faq.q: What standard covers safety harnesses?
faq.a: EN 361 for full-body fall-arrest harnesses — the only body-holding device rated for arresting a fall. Work-positioning belts and restraint systems fall under EN 358, energy-absorbing lanyards under EN 355, and retractable blocks under EN 360. All are Category III PPE with formal inspection duties.

faq.q: How often must fall arrest equipment be inspected?
faq.a: Pre-use checks every use, plus formal recorded inspection by a competent person at intervals the manufacturer and risk assessment set — at least every 12 months, and more often in harsh use. Anything that has arrested a fall is withdrawn immediately.

faq.q: What should you wear under a safety harness?
faq.a: Slim, fitted workwear layers that keep the harness geometry as designed: no bulky padding under leg straps, no loose hoods around the dorsal attachment, nothing covering or catching the buckles. The harness is set up over the clothing you'll actually work in — refit it when the season changes the layers.

pages.cardBlurb: C1 to C3 spray-operator clothing decoded — the standard agriculture never knew it had, and when disposables beat it.
pages.h1: EN ISO 27065: clothing for spray operators.
pages.metaTitle: EN ISO 27065 Explained: Pesticide Operator Clothing C1–C3 | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN ISO 27065 decoded — the C1, C2 and C3 protection levels for pesticide operator clothing, how it differs from general chemical suits, and how product labels drive what spray operators wear.
pages.lede: Most farm spraying happens in clothing chosen by habit, yet there's a dedicated standard for exactly this job: EN ISO 27065 grades operator clothing C1 to C3 against pesticide handling's real exposures. It's the missing link between 'old waterproofs' and full chemical suits — and the product label is what invokes it.

heroMeta.l: The product SDS names the kit
Certified garments that wash and return

blocks.html:
EN ISO 27065 certifies clothing specifically against liquid pesticide exposure — penetration and repellency of spray formulations rather than the industrial-chemical batteries of the EN 13034 world. C1 covers lower-exposure operation (cab work, incidental drift), C2 the standard operator level for mixing, loading and application, and C3 the highest exposures — handling concentrates, drenched conditions, knapsack work in crops. The garments are washable and re-certifiable through their stated care cycle, which is the standard's quiet advantage: purpose-made spray clothing that returns to service, versus the disposable-coverall habit that works but generates a bin-bag per tank mix.

What invokes it is the product label and safety data sheet — UK authorisation increasingly references 27065 levels for operator clothing, alongside the gauntlets, face protection and boots the label lists. The buying rule stays the one from our farm-worker guide: read the label of the product you're actually spraying; it names the level.

faq.q: What is EN ISO 27065 clothing?
faq.a: Clothing certified specifically for pesticide operators — tested against spray-formulation penetration at three levels: C1 (low exposure), C2 (standard mixing and application) and C3 (high exposure like concentrates and knapsack work). It's washable, re-usable spray kit; the pesticide product's label indicates the level required.

faq.q: Can you spray in disposable coveralls instead?
faq.a: Often yes — Type 4/6 disposables with the right chemical performance are a legitimate alternative where the product label allows, and they suit occasional spraying. Regular operators usually land on certified 27065 garments for comfort and cost-per-season, with disposables kept for the filthiest tasks.

faq.q: What PPE does a pesticide label require?
faq.a: The label and safety data sheet specify it per product — typically protective clothing (increasingly by 27065 level), nitrile gauntlets, face or eye protection and suitable boots, with extra RPE for some formulations. The label is a legal instruction, not a suggestion; certification for the operator comes via the spray-qualification system.

pages.cardBlurb: The test standard behind rental workwear and FR wash-life claims — what industrial laundering does to garments and how it's certified.
pages.metaTitle: EN ISO 15797 Explained: Industrial Laundering of Workwear | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN ISO 15797 decoded — the industrial laundering test standard behind rental workwear and FR wash-life claims, what tunnel washing does to garments, and what the marking means for buyers.
pages.lede: Industrial laundries are not big washing machines — they're 75-degree tunnel washers and cabinet dryers that would destroy a high-street garment in a fortnight. EN ISO 15797 is the standard that proves a garment survives that process, and it's the small print behind every rental contract and most FR wash-life claims.

blocks.h2: Testing for a harder life than home
blocks.html:
EN ISO 15797 defines reference industrial washing and drying procedures — high-temperature tunnel washes with industrial chemistry, followed by tumble or tunnel-finisher drying — and garments certified against it have survived those cycles with their dimensions, appearance and performance intact. For protective kit that last word is the whole point: an FR garment's wash-life claims and a hi-vis garment's colour endurance are stated against defined wash procedures, and 15797 is the industrial one. (The domestic equivalent, for home-washing claims, is ISO 6330 — the care label's world.)

Why buyers meet it: rental and laundry-service contracts effectively require 15797-capable garments — anything less falls apart in the tunnel and the contract. Direct buyers meet it as a durability signal: a garment built to survive industrial laundering is over-built for home washing in the best way, which is why our fabric guide treats the marking as a quality shorthand even for teams that will never use a tunnel washer.

head: Buyer
What 15797 means to you
rows: The garment is contract-viable — it survives the process your service uses

faq.q: What does industrially launderable mean?
faq.a: The garment is certified (typically to EN ISO 15797) to survive industrial laundry processes — high-temperature tunnel washing and industrial drying — without losing its fit, appearance or protective performance. It's the durability grade rental services and laundry contracts require.

faq.q: What's the difference between EN ISO 15797 and the care label?
faq.a: The care label reflects domestic washing (tested under ISO 6330); EN ISO 15797 covers industrial processes, which are hotter, more chemical and more mechanical. A garment can be home-washable but not industrial-grade — putting it through a tunnel washer anyway is how rental stock gets wrecked.

faq.q: Does industrial laundering damage workwear?
faq.a: It ages any garment faster than home washing — that's why the standard exists. Garments built to 15797 tolerate it by design; garments that aren't shrink, fade, delaminate and lose print quickly. For protective kit, the laundering method must match what the garment's performance claims were tested against.
